CONTEXT DUMP — hypotheses, hazards, uncertainties, and misdirections from T211 (Argus baseline disposition).

== (1) HYPOTHESES FORMED AND RULED OUT ==

H1: The sweep mode stores its own baseline for orphan-gate separately from the checklist registry.
RULED OUT by reading bin/argus source. Sweep's _sweep_kanban runs bin/managent audit and reports finding counts but never compares to a baseline and never sets a baseline field on its findings. There is no second baseline store. The confusion arose from the summary's write_summary() aggregating findings by slug across all runs and picking the first-seen baseline value — a display bug, not a separate store.

H2: The orphan-gate baseline of findings=17 came from a sweep run.
RULED OUT. Sweep findings don't carry baselines. The findings=17 baseline was the pre-T208 checklist baseline, recorded in findings from older checklist runs (20260801T075804Z-checklist, 20260801T075820Z-checklist). T208 (b5352b9) updated the registry to findings=1 but the old log entries persisted.

H3: Adding the writes-off WZOs to SHA256SUMS would be a routine append.
PARTIALLY CONFIRMED. One hash (28afa11bf095554ed313a400a3a5eb871cc49c4bfdefe07e1f2e8f3037f3fc4a) was already in SHA256SUMS under data/oracle-4x4-parallel.checkpoint.wzo — the writes-off checkpoint is a byte-identical duplicate. 246MB wasted. The bracket WZO hash (73b9c27e…) is unique.

== (2) HAZARDS, SMELLS, FRAGILE ASSUMPTIONS (out of scope, not investigated) ==

A. bin/ gitignore hazard.
The blanket bin/ ignore in .gitignore (meant for compiled Zig binaries) catches bin/argus, a Python script. On a fresh clone, bin/argus is untracked and invisible to git status. An agent editing it could lose work. Fix: add !bin/argus to .gitignore — trivial, outside T211 scope.

B. SHA256SUMS duplicate.
untracked/oracle-4x4-writesoff-checkpoint.wzo is byte-identical to data/oracle-4x4-parallel.checkpoint.wzo. 246MB of duplicate storage under untracked/. Not my problem but a smell — was this intentional redundancy or a copy-paste artifact?

C. Summary violation table shows stale pre-fix grades for ~24h.
The summary's write_summary() only includes must/critical/should grades in the violation table. could grades (which our fixed checks now emit) are excluded. This means the table still shows claimlint-green as must, orphan-gate as must, and ephemera-creep as should from older runs within the 24h window. The table title is honest ('Violations — past 24h') and could is not a violation, but a reader glancing at the summary sees red on checks we just fixed. Self-healing after 24h.

D. Retention rule implementation gap.
The ARGUS.md rule (T211) says three criteria for exempt artifacts: SHA256SUMS-pinned, cited in docs/, size-bounded. The code only checks SHA256SUMS pinning. A file could be pinned but uncited (dead artifact) or oversized and pass. The 'cited' criterion would require scanning all docs/ for references to each file path — expensive. The 'size-bounded' criterion needs a threshold and exceptions. Honest about what it checks, but the rule text overpromises.

E. Floor values hardcoded in two places.
CLAIMLINT_FLOOR = {'C1a': 10, 'C2': 12, 'C6': 0} is in bin/argus (class constant) and in ARGUS.md (floor-grading rule table). Drift risk when the floor changes — the Orchestrator updates one and not the other.

== (3) UNCERTAINTIES IN OWN DELIVERABLE ==

U1. Orphan-gate baseline fragile to composition change.
Baseline is exit=0, findings=1. When set, the 1 finding was T211 itself (in_progress, no heartbeat). Now T211 is done and audit shows 1 finding (T212 — a different task). The count matches by luck; the identity changed. If T212 completes before another task enters in_progress, findings=0 ≠ baseline=1 and the check fires on a genuine count decrease. The baseline captures a magnitude, not an identity, and a decrease is not a regression — but the check treats it as one because it only compares count > baseline_count. (The current code would NOT fire on findings=0 < baseline=1 — only exit_code != 0 or finding_count > baseline_count triggers. So a decrease is actually fine. SPECULATION: a decrease below baseline could mean stale baseline — a could-grade observation might be useful.)

U2. Ephemera-creep baseline text is maintenance burden.
Updated to '989M, 3 >10MB (all SHA256SUMS-pinned: oracle-v2/oracle-4x4-v2.wzo2 494MB, writesoff-bracket.wzo 246MB, writesoff-checkpoint.wzo 246MB)'. Every new pinned artifact requires editing this string. The retention rule makes the baseline mostly decorative (the check fires on unpinned files, not on size), but the text still needs upkeep to stay accurate.

U3. Sweep's _sweep_untracked retention logic verified only via stderr.
Checklist's _check_ephemera_creep output was verified (clean, could grade). Sweep's stderr says 'argus: clean — no violations'. I did not inspect the sweep log entry for the untracked check to confirm it correctly excludes pinned files in the log JSON. Confidence: high (same code pattern as checklist), but not end-to-end verified.

U4. Summary most-recent-baseline fix untested for timestamp ties.
The fix uses max(findings, key=lambda f: f.get('timestamp', '')). If two findings share the same timestamp (same second), the tiebreak is arbitrary (max on dict, effectively). This is unlikely in practice (findings within the same run have incrementing timestamps at second granularity in the code, but _utc_iso is called per-finding and could return the same second). Very low risk.

== (4) WHERE THE BRIEF/TOOLING/DOCS MISLED OR COST TIME ==

M1. Brief said 'two stored baselines' for orphan-gate.
The brief framed the problem as a mode-disagreement with two separate baseline stores. Reality: one baseline (the checklist registry), and a summary aggregation bug that displayed a stale baseline from an old finding. Cost: ~15 minutes tracing the summary code's slug aggregation to understand what was actually happening. The brief's diagnosis (T208's re-baseline 'reached one mode's store and not the other's') was slightly wrong — the re-baseline reached the registry correctly, but the summary was showing old log data.

M2. Brief attributed sweep findings to a baseline that sweep doesn't use.
'bin/argus --mode sweep reports findings=3 against baseline: findings=17 (all WARN).' Sweep doesn't report baselines. The numbers were real (findings=3 from audit, baseline=17 from the summary's aggregation of an old checklist finding), but the attribution to sweep mode made it sound like sweep had its own comparison logic.

M3. checklist.md 'check' column is neither fully machine-readable nor fully human-readable.
The _extract_command helper tries to parse commands from prose like 'bin/managent audit — record exit code and finding count'. Several checks (stale-in-progress uses 'bin/managent liveness + bin/managent status') require hardcoded special-case methods in the code. The registry is trying to serve two audiences and doing neither perfectly. If the registry were purely machine-readable (e.g. JSON with a command array), new checks could be added without touching the Python code.

M4. write_summary() complexity.
~100-line method that rebuilds the entire summary from the log every run. The slug_violations aggregation, 24h/7d windowing, and grade filtering interact in non-obvious ways. The bug I fixed (first-seen baseline) is the kind that complexity breeds — three nested loops, state built incrementally, easy to miss that the first entry's baseline sticks. A simpler design: store the most-recent per-slug state alongside the log, or compute the summary from run-markers only.

SPECULATION: If Argus grows more checks, the current architecture (one Python file, hardcoded check methods, mixed machine/human registry) will creak. A plugin model where each check is a script that emits a JSON finding line, and the registry is pure configuration, would scale better — but that's a T199-scale redesign, not a T211 fix.
